items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' The call opens 'Hello, this is Frank. How can I help you?' and the structure after that is entirely customer-driven — she asks about the hourly rate, he asks for a date, she asks again. A roadmap ('let me get a few details, then I'll walk you through pricing and we'll have you a number in about ten minutes — sound good?') would have shortened a twenty-minute call on an 800 square foot one-bedroom moving two floors inside the same building.
Never asked how she was. She opened with 'Hi, good morning Frank, sorry got allergies' — an explicit cue, and it drew 'That's okay. Okay. Correct, yes.'
Additional rooms never probed — no garage, no storage unit, no patio or balcony question, on an apartment move where the balcony contents are a routine surprise.

Access concerns only half-covered. The elevator came up because she raised it ('the elevator is really pretty close'), and she volunteered 'we don't have to worry about the loading dock in each building.' Frank never asked whether the elevator needs to be reserved for the move window, never mentioned a certificate of insurance, and never asked whether the fourth-floor unit will be ready on October 1 — on a property where Einstein has a standing partnership and he is on first-name terms with the office ('we usually speak to Audrey or Lily there at the office'). He had a direct line to answer all three and used it for rapport instead.

The clock start was never explained. He covered the minimum and the proration — 'we do prorate in fifteen minute increments. So we have the two and a half hour minimum and then we prorate in fifteen minutes from there' — but never said when billable time begins or ends. On a same-building move where the crew will be walking between two units rather than driving, 'the clock starts when we arrive and stops after the final walkthrough at the new unit' is the sentence that prevents a day-of dispute.
No sense-check anywhere in the pricing or clock explanation.

The 'pricing is super simple' opener was replaced with 'so we have variable pricing,' which is the opposite framing. She had already asked the rate question twice by that point and was told instead that it depends on the day and that he needed her date first. The rate did not arrive until several minutes later.

The what's-included list was thin: 'we're gonna have all the moving blankets. So all the tools, everything necessary to complete the move and that's all included in the hourly rate.' Gas, truck, taxes and insurance were never named.

No Worries Damage Coverage was never mentioned — not once, in twenty minutes, to a customer whose entire stated anxiety is irreplaceable fragile possessions. She raised it three separate times: 'I love my older items and I have a couple of items that they need to be handled with special care'; 'I have a special Asian table that the top is removable but it has a marble center and they're all very delicate as well. I've spent so much money as well. I've traveled a lot on repair'; and the trundle bed 'I've had it from California to Colorado and back again to Austin. I've got so much invested in it right now. I'm not gonna give it up.' Three explicit invitations to say 'and every move includes up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse accidental damage, at no extra charge' and it never came. This is the single most expensive miss on the call.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned — on a self-described senior customer moving alone, who said 'family cannot support me right now' and 'I cannot physically be in two places at one,' and who explicitly said 'I still prefer the human contact.' Knowing her mover's name and face before the day is worth more to this customer than to almost anyone else in the sample.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, despite her asking specifically for a morning start — 'Do you feel like we can possibly have a morning situation?' — and being given an 8:30 AM commitment.

The specialty items she flagged were acknowledged warmly but never priced into the time. The iron trundle bed 'has screws in detail so that will be time consuming' — her words — plus a marble-top table requiring separate handling, and neither added a minute to the estimate.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used to make the hours feel concrete.

Save Your Ass speech almost entirely absent. The one line in its territory came early — 'it just depends on how much you want us to move and what you want to move yourself if you're trying to keep costs down' — and she immediately closed that door: 'unfortunately, I'm the senior, obviously I'm not gonna be doing a lot of transporting myself.' Frank correctly dropped the carload tip, but then dropped the whole section with it. The prep half still applied and would have helped her more than anyone: she is moving inside one building, she has roughly 35 boxes, and she has a friend who was going to stand around in the new unit watching. Staging boxes by the door, emptying the trundle bed's drawers, and having the friend receive and direct at the fourth floor instead of spectating are all real time savers, and none were mentioned.

No bolded-details framing on the confirmation email — which matters unusually much here, because she is uncertain about the destination unit number ('I'm thinking 4127 but I can correct all that stuff') and her box count is a guess she has promised to update.

Hours of operation never given. He gave her a good callback path — reply to the email, or call in and give the office your email address — but never said when the office is open, to a customer who said outright she prefers talking to a person.
Customer's name used once, and only in the form of a question — 'caller ID says Margaret Renee is that your full name?' She used his name twice. He never used hers again.
top_strength: Frank read this customer correctly and sold to the thing she was actually buying, which was not a price. Margaret is a senior moving alone inside one building, and the fear underneath every one of her tangents is that she will have to be in two places at once and something will go wrong while she is not looking. She asked him directly: 'I have one friend but I thought she might stay in the new location to watch the process. Any thoughts or what do I do? Do I have to hire a third person? It's kinda hard for me to be in two places. I just kinda wonder if you have any thoughts or advice. I haven't done this before.' Instead of answering the literal question, Frank walked her through the day so that the question dissolved: 'my movers are gonna want to do final walkthroughs with you at each end of it. We're gonna walk with you when we first get there, even though it's 800 square feet we're going to go to every corner of that place before we start and then we're gonna tell you what we're gonna do. We're gonna start wrapping everything. The guys are gonna go to the new place, everything's gonna start getting loaded in there... and then before we leave the job site we're gonna walk with you at your current place to make sure we got everything and then we're gonna walk with you at the ending place to make sure everything is exactly where you want it.' Then the reframe that actually closed it: 'the guys will be at your disposal. You just tell them exactly what you need. So you can lean on us, we are your help. We're in business to make sure you're less stressed on move day.' Her response measures the result: 'from what you're saying I think I'm feeling a little less apprehensive.' That is an objection about physical capability and loneliness resolved without a discount, without a third mover, and without ever naming the fear out loud. He also built real rapport off the property connection rather than reciting a script — 'we have a partnership with Everly. Yeah, we usually speak to Audrey or Lily there at the office' and 'I think even one of our owners' grandmother stays there as well' — which is the moment the call turned from a price inquiry into a conversation. And two mechanical things he did that most of this week's sample did not: he asked the walk-distance question explicitly ('how about walking distance from your current place to the new place? How long of a walk you think that'd be?'), and he closed the booking and the email in the same move, then invited corrections: 'you can always just update us on the room number if that's incorrect' and 'you can just reply back to the email I just sent over.' He also never let her apologize for rambling — 'No, you're fine. You're totally fine' and 'Oh, that's totally fine' — which on a twenty-minute call with an anxious customer is why she kept talking and why he got the booking.
coaching_note: Frank booked this move and earned it on trust, so the coaching here is about what he left on the table rather than what he got wrong. Highest-leverage fix: he never mentioned No Worries Damage Coverage, and this is the single best No Worries call in the whole week's sample. Margaret raised fragile irreplaceable items three separate times — the marble-center Asian table she has paid to repair before, the iron trundle bed she has hauled from California to Colorado to Austin and 'is not gonna give up,' and a general 'I love my older things.' Every one of those got 'Yeah, not a problem. We're going to be wrapping and protecting everything you own.' Wrapping is a process promise; No Worries is a financial promise, and it is the one that answers 'what happens if you break it anyway.' The line to add, right after she names the first delicate item: 'And I want you to know what stands behind that — every Einstein move includes No Worries Damage Coverage, up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse accidental damage, and it's already in the rate. Most movers cover you at sixty cents a pound, which on a marble tabletop is a few dollars. Ours covers the actual item.' Pair it with Meet Your Mover on this customer specifically — she said she prefers human contact and has no family nearby, and 'a few days before, you'll get an email with your mover's photo and name so you know exactly who's knocking' is worth more to her than a weekday discount. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-four review, and this one is the underestimate side of the pattern rather than the padding side. Frank stated the typical range as 'anywhere between two and a half to three and a half hours' and then said 'since you're in the same building, I'll just take the average there and just call it a three hour estimate' — before he had learned any of the things that make this move slower than average. After that line he found out there are roughly 35 boxes including four heavy Home Depot mediums, an iron trundle bed that she herself said 'has screws in detail so that will be time consuming,' a marble-top table needing separate handling, a fourth-floor destination reached by elevator, and a mirror-image floor plan that will slow placement. He also learned the customer is a senior moving alone who will be directing placement herself. None of it moved the number. The customer then told him the estimate was wrong: 'I honestly feel certain that there's no way it's gonna be under three hours honestly.' She is almost certainly right. Same-building does not mean fast — it means no drive time and a lot of elevator trips, and elevator trips are where apartment moves quietly overrun. This is exactly the apartment-underestimate half of the 46 percent problem: the assumption that a short distance means a short move. The fix is a sentence, not a rebuild: 'With the trundle bed disassembly and about 35 boxes going up to the fourth floor, I'd plan for the top of that range — call it three and a half, maybe four. You only pay for the time we use, so if we beat it you pay less, but I'd rather set your expectation high than low.' That is more accurate, it is more honest, and on this customer it would have built trust rather than cost the sale. Third, smaller: fill in the clock start and add a sense-check. 'The clock starts when we arrive and open the contract, and it stops after we walk the new place with you — does that make sense?' takes four seconds and closes the one mechanical gap in an otherwise well-run call. And use her name. He said 'Margaret Renee' once as a caller-ID question and never again, while she used his twice and thanked him by name at the close.
phone_presence_notes: Genuinely patient and reassuring with a customer who interrupted herself constantly and apologized for it four separate times — he shut down every apology ('No, you're fine. You're totally fine', 'Oh, that's totally fine'), built real unscripted rapport off the shared property connection, and reframed her core anxiety into a concrete walkthrough narrative that visibly worked ('I'm feeling a little less apprehensive'); short of a 5 only because he never once used her name and a great deal of his side is bare 'Yeah. Right. Okay. Gotcha.' filler while she carried the conversation.
